content.text:
## Bottom line

**This is a good, market-rate L6 offer, but not an exceptional “leave a job you like” offer. I would negotiate rather than accept or walk immediately.**

Assuming the $1.08M grant vests evenly over four years and the stock price stays constant:

|  | Meta | Google offer |
|---|---:|---:|
| Base | $240K | $235K |
| Target bonus | $36K | $47K |
| Annual initial-grant vesting | ~$250K normally; $200K next 12 months | $270K |
| Target annual TC | ~$526K | **$552K** |
| Next-12-month comparison | ~$476K | **$552K** |

Google’s offer is approximately:

- **$26K/year, or 5%, above** your stated normal Meta compensation.
- **$76K above** your unusual next-12-month Meta number.
- Almost exactly the current reported median for an SF Bay Area Google L6 PM—Levels.fyi presently reports approximately **$551K**. ([levels.fyi](https://www.levels.fyi/companies/google/salaries/product-manager/locations/san-francisco-bay-area))
- Only modestly above the midpoint of the posted base range. Your $235K base is at approximately the **59th percentile of the listed band**, with substantial room up to $271K.

For someone happy at Meta who was not looking, **a 5% guaranteed premium is not enough by itself to compensate for switching risk, lost organizational capital, uncertain performance calibration, and uncertain refresh grants.**

## Don’t count the refresh grants at full value

The recruiter’s illustration produces this equity schedule, assuming straight-line vesting:

| Year | Initial grant vesting | Refresh vesting | Total Google equity |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 | $270K | $0 | $270K |
| 2 | $270K | $62.5K | $332.5K |
| 3 | $270K | $125K | $395K |
| 4 | $270K | $187.5K | $457.5K |
| 5 onward | $0 | ~$250K | ~$250K |

That gives approximate Google TC of:

- Year 1: **$552K**
- Year 2: **$614.5K**
- Year 3: **$677K**
- Year 4: **$739.5K**
- Year 5 steady state: **$532K**

Over the first four years:

- **No refreshes:** $2.208M, or $552K/year average
- **Full illustrated refreshes:** $2.583M, or approximately $646K/year average

But you should not compare “Google with all illustrative refreshes” against “Meta with no future refreshes.” Google officially says equity refresh amounts depend on inputs including performance, location and role, with manager discretion and higher-level review. ([services.google.com](https://services.google.com/fh/files/blogs/pay_equity_info_sheet.pdf))

For your decision model, I would use three scenarios:

1. **Downside:** zero refreshes.
2. **Planning case:** 50% of the recruiter’s illustration.
3. **Upside:** 100% of the illustration.

At 50% credit, Google averages approximately **$599K/year over four years**. Then separately model whatever refreshes you reasonably expect at Meta.

## First, verify the vesting schedule

This is critical. The recruiter’s arithmetic appears to assume 25% per year, but reported Google vesting schedules include multiple possibilities, including a front-loaded 38%/32%/20%/10% schedule. ([levels.fyi](https://www.levels.fyi/companies/google/salaries/product-manager/locations/san-francisco-bay-area))

Ask for written confirmation of:

1. The exact annual vesting percentages on the $1.08M grant.
2. Monthly versus quarterly vesting and the first vest date.
3. The share-price/grant-date methodology.
4. Whether you will be eligible for the next annual refresh cycle.
5. When refresh grants begin vesting.
6. Whether your first bonus is prorated.
7. Whether starting later would affect bonus or refresh eligibility.

If the grant is front-loaded, the four-year total is unchanged but the recruiter’s year-by-year illustration is wrong. For example, 38%/32%/20%/10% would produce initial-grant vesting of roughly:

- Year 1: $410K
- Year 2: $346K
- Year 3: $216K
- Year 4: $108K

That creates a very different retention cliff and refresh interaction.

## What I would ask for

### Opening counter

Ask for:

- **Base: $260,000**
- **New-hire equity: $1,400,000**
- **Sign-on bonus: $100,000**

At straight-line vesting, that is:

- $260K base
- $52K target bonus
- $350K annual initial equity
- **$662K recurring target TC**
- **$762K first year including sign-on**

That is an anchor, not necessarily your expected outcome. It is defensible because:

- You already make approximately $526K.
- You are happy and not actively looking.
- The current offer provides only a small guaranteed premium.
- The posted base ceiling is $271K.
- Google apparently has room to use signing bonuses; current Levels.fyi data identifies signing bonuses as variable and reports $50K as the PM median among relevant submissions. ([levels.fyi](https://www.levels.fyi/companies/google/salaries/product-manager/locations/san-francisco-bay-area))

### Good settlement range

I would consider this a meaningful improvement:

- **Base: $250K–$255K**
- **New-hire equity: $1.25M–$1.35M**
- **Sign-on: $50K–$100K**

For example, $255K base, $1.3M equity and a $75K sign-on produces:

- Base: $255K
- Bonus: $51K
- Initial equity: $325K/year
- Recurring TC: **$631K**
- First year: **$706K**
- Four-year average before refreshes: approximately **$650K**, including the sign-on

That is much more appropriate for persuading a happy, highly compensated candidate to leave.

## Prioritize the components this way

### 1. Initial equity

This is the most important request. An increase from $1.08M to:

- $1.20M adds $30K/year over four years.
- $1.30M adds $55K/year.
- $1.40M adds $80K/year.

A $1.30M grant would get the recurring package to approximately **$607K** even if base remains $235K.

### 2. Sign-on bonus

There is currently no transition compensation. Ask for $100K, especially if you will forfeit a specific Meta vest or annual bonus by leaving on Google’s preferred start date.

If you have a large Meta vest shortly before the proposed start date, the easiest solution may be:

- Delay your Google start date until after that vest, or
- Request a dollar-for-dollar cash make-whole for the specific amount lost.

Do not describe the entire $200K vesting over the next year as an immediate loss; Google will correctly point out that its own equity vests during that same period. Focus on compensation actually forfeited because of the exact departure date.

### 3. Base

Ask for $260K but expect more resistance here. Base bands and internal parity are usually tighter. Because bonus is 20% of base, every $10K increase in base adds another $2K in target bonus.

If they say base is capped, respond:

> Understood. In that case, could we focus on increasing the initial equity grant and adding a sign-on bonus?

## Suggested script

> I’m genuinely excited about the team and role. At the same time, I wasn’t actively looking, I’m happy at Meta, and my current annual compensation is approximately $526,000.  
>  
> The current offer is roughly $552,000 annually before any refreshes, so the guaranteed premium is relatively modest given the risk and opportunity cost of changing companies. I also understand that refresh grants are discretionary, so I can’t treat the illustrative refresh amounts as guaranteed compensation.  
>  
> To make the move compelling, I’d like to see whether the team can get closer to a $260,000 base, a $1.4 million initial equity grant, and a $100,000 sign-on bonus. I’m flexible on the mix—if base is constrained, my priorities would be the equity grant and sign-on bonus.  
>  
> Could you take that package back to compensation and see what flexibility is available?

If asked what would close you:

> A package in the neighborhood of $255,000 base, $1.3 million in equity and a meaningful sign-on bonus would make the decision substantially easier.

Only say you will sign at that number if you really will.

## Accept, negotiate or walk?

### My recommendation: **Negotiate**

You have excellent leverage:

- You have a strong existing job.
- Your current compensation is documented.
- You did not initiate the search.
- Google has already invested in interviewing and approving you.
- There is visible room within the posted base range.
- There is no sign-on bonus in the initial offer.

### If they improve materially

Accept if:

- You prefer or are genuinely excited about the Google role and manager,
- The vesting and refresh timing check out, and
- Guaranteed four-year compensation reaches roughly **$600K–$625K per year before speculative refreshes**, or the role offers a major career advantage.

### If they leave the offer unchanged

I would probably **stay at Meta**, unless:

- The Google role is substantially better in scope, product area, manager quality or promotion prospects;
- Your Meta equity is approaching a significant cliff; or
- You specifically want to diversify your career away from Meta.

As written, the offer is fair enough for someone already motivated to leave. It is not yet strong enough to buy a happy IC6 away primarily on compensation. The right move is one firm, professionally framed counter—not an immediate rejection.

content.text:
## My recommendation

**Yes—assuming you’re at least reasonably positive about the role, manager, and team, I would take this offer.**

The $200K sign-on materially changes the decision. The original package was only modestly better than Meta; the final package gives you substantial first-year protection and a meaningful four-year premium even if Google gives you **zero refresh grants**.

## Compensation comparison

Assuming the $1.08M grant vests evenly over four years:

|  | Stay at Meta | Join Google |
|---|---:|---:|
| Base | $240K | $240K |
| Target bonus | $36K | $48K |
| Equity in next 12 months | $200K | $270K |
| Sign-on | — | $200K |
| **First-year target compensation** | **$476K** | **$758K** |

That is a **$282K pre-tax first-year advantage** for Google. 

After the sign-on year, and assuming no refreshes:

- Meta normal annual TC: **approximately $526K**
- Google annual TC: **approximately $558K**
- Google advantage: **approximately $32K/year**

Over four years, before any Google refreshes:

- Google: **$2.432M**
- Meta, using $476K next year and $526K for the following three: **$2.054M**
- Google advantage: **approximately $378K**
- Google four-year average: **approximately $608K/year** 

Alphabet reports that its RSUs generally vest over four years and require continued employment through each vesting date. ([abc.xyz](https://abc.xyz/assets/99/21/46cafdba41089a12a2d86ea47d44/goog026-annualreport2024-web.pdf?utm_source=openai))

## The important distinction

The $200K sign-on is not merely replacing the Meta RSUs you’re forfeiting.

You are giving up $200K of Meta RSUs but receiving during the first year:

- $270K of Google RSUs
- $200K sign-on
- $12K more target bonus
- The same base salary

So Google isn’t just making you whole. It is paying a meaningful switching premium.

## How I’d think about the refreshes

Treat refresh grants as upside, not as part of the reason to accept.

Using the recruiter’s illustration:

- **Zero refreshes:** four-year Google average of $608K
- **Half the illustrated refreshes:** approximately $655K
- **Full illustrated refreshes:** approximately $702K

The earlier $646K estimate excluded the new sign-on; adding the $200K sign-on increases the four-year average by $50K.

One correction to the recruiter’s long-term framing: the $250K “steady-state” refresh amount refers to the eventual annual vesting produced by several overlapping grants. You should not assume that value until grants have actually been awarded.

## When I would not take it

I would still stay at Meta if one or more of these is true:

1. **The Google manager or product area concerns you.**
2. The Google role has materially less scope or weaker promotion prospects.
3. You expect a Meta promotion or major refresh soon that would close most of the four-year gap.
4. You place unusually high value on your established Meta reputation, team, flexibility, or work-life balance.
5. The sign-on has an unusually onerous repayment requirement.
6. You believe you are at meaningful layoff or performance-management risk in the new role.

This remains partly a career decision because, after year one, Google’s no-refresh premium is only about **6%**. The $200K sign-on makes the four-year economics attractive, but it does not make a bad job worth taking.

## Verify these terms before signing

Get written answers on:

- **Sign-on payment date**
- **Clawback period:** commonly the key issue
- Whether repayment is full or prorated if you leave
- Whether repayment is based on the **gross** $200K even though you receive a smaller net payment
- Exact RSU vesting schedule and first vest date
- Whether the first annual bonus is prorated
- Eligibility for the next refresh cycle
- Any start-date cutoff affecting bonus or refresh eligibility

Also, do not confuse bonus withholding with final tax liability. Separately paid supplemental wages can be subject to 22% federal withholding in many circumstances, but your ultimate tax is determined on your full return and may be higher at your income level. ([irs.gov](https://www.irs.gov/publications/p15?utm_source=openai))

### One especially important issue

If the sign-on requires full repayment for two years, mentally treat it as:

- $100K earned after year one
- Another $100K earned after year two

If it is fully forgiven after one year, it is substantially more attractive. If possible, ask for **monthly prorated repayment** even if they will not increase the headline offer. That is not necessarily reopening compensation; it is clarifying or improving a contractual term.

## Final decision

**On compensation alone: take it.**

Your negotiation worked. Google moved the package from roughly market-rate to a compelling four-year offer:

- Same base as Meta
- Higher target bonus
- Higher initial annual equity
- $200K cash switching premium
- Refresh upside that you do not need to assume for the economics to work

My decision rule would be:

> **If I would rate the Google role, manager and team at least 7/10, I would accept. If I have serious reservations about them, I would stay at Meta rather than let the one-time $200K override those concerns.**

Since they have called it their best offer, I would not counter again on headline compensation. I would verify the vesting, bonus, refresh-eligibility and clawback terms, then accept if those are reasonable.
